theme: Praise the LORD, all nations, the shortest psalm; widest vision
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 117. It has only two verses. Read it three times, slowly, once for each phrase of the call, and notice how much is packed into so few words.
settingTheScene: Psalm 117 is the shortest chapter in the Bible and the middle chapter of the Bible’s chapters, by number. It is part of the Hallel, sung at the feasts. In two verses it calls the whole world to praise the God of Israel, and gives the reason. Paul quotes it in Romans 15 to show that the Gentiles were always meant to glorify God.
interpretation:
The psalm is short, but it is wide. The call is not to Israel only but to “all nations” and “all peoples.” Under the old covenant, God’s saving work was centered on one nation. But from the beginning, the aim was the world. God promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed. The psalmists often sing of a day when the nations will bow. Psalm 117 states it as a command: praise the LORD, all of you.

Notice the reason: “For great is his steadfast love toward us.” The word “us” is Israel, the people who knew God’s covenant love. The nations are called to praise him because of what he has done for his people. When the nations see the LORD’s love to Israel, they are drawn to worship. And the Gentiles who come in are included in the “us” by faith.

The two characteristics that the psalm names are the two that run through the whole Old Testament: steadfast love and faithfulness. They were revealed to Moses on Sinai (“abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness”) and they are the foundation of the covenant. God does not just love; he keeps his word. His faithfulness “endures forever.”

This is the Bible in miniature: the LORD’s love for his people, his faithfulness through time, and his purpose for the world. Luke’s Gospel carries the same note. Simeon sang of a light for the Gentiles. John the Baptist quoted Isaiah, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Jesus will praise the faith of a Roman centurion. The psalm that told the nations to sing is being fulfilled in the church today, as people from every tribe and language come to Christ.
connection: Genesis 12:3 promised blessing to all the families of the earth. Exodus 34:6 states the LORD’s character. Psalm 67 prays that all the nations praise him. Isaiah 49:6 speaks of salvation to the end of the earth. Luke 2:32 echoes it. Romans 15:11 quotes this psalm. Revelation 7:9 pictures a great multitude from every nation, praising God.
application:
Read the psalm aloud in a different voice each time: quietly, with joy, and as a shout.

Pray for one nation or people group by name today, that they would praise the LORD.

Memorize the two verses. They are the shortest way to remember what God’s love and faithfulness mean.
prayerPrompts: Praise God with all the nations in your own words.
Thank him for his great steadfast love toward us.
Pray for the nations to know him.
